title: Remote Pilot (Part 107 Drone)
summary: Free ground school for the FAA Remote Pilot knowledge test (UAG): operating rules, airspace and LAANC, charts, weather, loading, Remote ID, night and over-people flights, and decision making.
who: This course is for anyone who wants to fly a drone under 14 CFR Part 107, which covers most work done for pay or for a business, and for anyone who wants the certificate for its own sake. The remote pilot certificate with a small UAS rating lets you fly small unmanned aircraft (under 55 pounds) under the Part 107 rules. It needs no medical exam, no flight test and no flying hours. You pass one 60-question knowledge test, or, if you already hold a Part 61 pilot certificate, you finish free online training. You then keep the certificate current with free online recurrent training every 24 calendar months. The course follows the FAA Remote Pilot Small UAS Airman Certification Standards.

facts.value: 14 calendar days after a failure, no endorsement

facts.value: None. You must not know of a condition that would interfere with safe operation

facts.value: Free online recurrent training within each 24 calendar months

facts.label: Aircraft weight
facts.value: Less than 55 pounds on takeoff, including everything on board

facts.label: Flight limits
facts.value: 400 feet AGL, 87 knots groundspeed, 3 statute miles, 500 feet below and 2,000 feet from clouds

notes: The test is called Unmanned Aircraft General, Small (UAG). Every question is multiple choice with one correct answer.
You must be at least 14 to sit for the test and at least 16 to hold the certificate. The date of birth on your ID must show you meet the age rule before the test report expires.
No instructor endorsement is needed to take the test or to retake it. After a failure you wait 14 calendar days and bring the failed test report.
Get an FAA Tracking Number (FTN) by creating an IACRA account before you book. Then schedule the test with an FAA-approved testing center and arrange payment with the center.
Bring government-issued photo identification that shows your photo, signature, date of birth and permanent mailing address. If the address is a post office box, also bring a residential address.
The testing center gives you a supplement book with the charts and figures the questions use. Written notes are not allowed.
Your test report lists the codes of the questions you missed. Apply in IACRA soon after you pass, because the report has an expiration date.

requirements.text: Be able to read, speak, write and understand English. The FAA may add limits to the certificate if a medical reason keeps you from meeting one of these.
Not know, or have reason to know, of a physical or mental condition that would interfere with the safe operation of a small UAS.

Show aeronautical knowledge by passing the initial knowledge test (UAG), or, if you hold a Part 61 pilot certificate (not a student certificate) and a current flight review, by completing the FAA's Part 107 initial training.
Pass the TSA security background check that the FAA runs as part of processing your application.

requirements.text: Do not have a drug or alcohol offense, or a refusal of an alcohol test, that gives the FAA grounds to deny the application.
Register each aircraft you fly under Part 107 and make sure it meets the Remote ID rule.

plan.focus: Learn the certificate process and the rules that make up the largest share of the test. Read the Part 107 operating rules slowly, then the over-people, night and Remote ID rules. Take the first practice test at the end of the week and note every missed topic.

Airspace, charts and airports. Practice reading chart pieces every day: classes, floors and ceilings, airports, obstacles and latitude and longitude. Learn the airport lights, markings and radio calls.
Weather, loading and emergencies. Decode five METARs and TAFs a day. Work the load factor and density altitude questions. Learn battery safety and the preflight checklist.

Decision making and human factors, then review. Take two full practice tests, read the sample questions from the FAA, and re-read the modules for every area you missed. Book the real test for the end of the week.

modules.title: The Remote Pilot Certificate, the Test and Staying Current
modules.summary: Who can hold the certificate, how the 60-question UAG test works, how to apply, and how to keep your privileges valid with recurrent training.
objectives: Say who needs a remote pilot certificate and who can hold one.
Describe the Unmanned Aircraft General (UAG) test: length, time limit, passing score and topic mix.
List the steps from a test appointment to the plastic card in your wallet.
Explain the shortcut for pilots who already hold a Part 61 certificate.
Explain the 24 calendar month rule and the free recurrent training.
Say what you must carry, show and report after you are certificated.

sections.heading: What the certificate is and who needs it
points: Part 107 is the rule book for civil small unmanned aircraft: aircraft that weigh less than 55 pounds on takeoff, counting everything on board. The pilot credential is called a remote pilot certificate with a small UAS rating.
A flight that is purely for fun can follow the recreational exception instead. Flights that are not purely recreational, which includes most work done for pay or for a business, fall under Part 107.
The certificate has no medical exam, no flight test and no minimum flight hours. It proves one thing: you passed an FAA knowledge test, or you finished the FAA training that replaces it.
A person without a certificate may touch the controls only while a certificated remote pilot in command directly supervises and can take over at once.

sections.heading: Eligibility rules
points: You must be at least 16 years old to hold the certificate. You must read, speak, write and understand English. The FAA can add limits to the certificate if a medical reason keeps you from meeting one of those language skills.

You must not know of any physical or mental condition that would interfere with safe operation of a small UAS. There is no medical certificate, so this is a promise you keep honestly before every flight.

A conviction for a drug law violation can lead to denial of an application for up to 1 year, or to suspension or revocation of a certificate. So can breaking the alcohol and drug flight rules, and so can refusing a required alcohol test.
Cheating on a knowledge test bans you from taking any FAA test or applying for any FAA certificate for 1 year, and it can cost you a certificate you already hold.

sections.heading: The knowledge test (UAG)
points: The test is called Unmanned Aircraft General, Small, or UAG. It has 60 multiple-choice questions, gives you 2 hours, and needs a score of 70 percent, which is 42 correct answers. Each question has one right answer.

You can sit for the test at age 14, but the certificate itself needs age 16. Your photo ID must show your photo, signature, date of birth and permanent mailing address. The date of birth must show you will meet the age rule before the test report expires.
No instructor endorsement is needed to take the test, and none is needed to retake it. After a failure you wait 14 calendar days and show the failed test report at the testing center.

The test centers hand you a supplement book with the charts and figures that some questions refer to. You may not bring written notes. The score report lists the ACS codes of the questions you missed, so you can aim your review.

The questions follow the Remote Pilot ACS. Its approximate weights are: regulations 15 to 25 percent, airspace 15 to 25 percent, weather 11 to 16 percent, loading and performance 7 to 11 percent, and operations 35 to 45 percent.

sections.heading: From test appointment to card
points: Step 1: Create an account in IACRA, the FAA's online application system. That gives you an FAA Tracking Number (FTN). Do this before you register for the test.
Step 2: Schedule the UAG at an FAA-approved testing center and bring your photo ID. Step 3: Pass the test.
Step 4: In IACRA, start a new application for a Remote Pilot certificate (FAA Form 8710-13) and enter the 17-digit exam ID from your test report. The exam can take up to 48 hours to show up.

Step 5: The FAA's partner agency, TSA, completes a security background check. You then receive an email with instructions for printing a temporary certificate. A temporary certificate is good for up to 120 calendar days.
Step 6: The permanent plastic card arrives by mail after the FAA finishes its processing.

sections.heading: The shortcut for Part 61 pilots
points: A person who holds a pilot certificate under Part 61, other than a student certificate, and who has a current flight review under 14 CFR 61.56, can skip the test. Instead the pilot completes the free online course Part 107 Small UAS Initial (ALC-451) on FAASafety.gov.

That training covers eight areas: Part 107 privileges and rules, weather effects on performance, loading, emergency procedures, crew resource management, performance, maintenance and preflight inspection, and night operations.

The pilot then fills out the application in IACRA and meets in person with a certifying official to prove identity. The official can be an FAA Flight Standards office, a designated pilot examiner, an airman certification representative or a certificated flight instructor. A flight instructor cannot issue a temporary certificate.

sections.heading: Staying current: 24 calendar months
points: You may not use the privileges of a remote pilot in command unless, within the previous 24 calendar months, you passed the initial test or completed recurrent training. A Part 61 pilot with a current flight review can use the Part 61 training course for the same purpose.
Count calendar months, not days. Example from the FAA's advisory circular: a pilot who passes the test on September 13 must finish recurrent training by the end of September, 24 months later.

Recurrent training today is a free online course on FAASafety.gov. Every certificate holder can take Part 107 Small UAS Recurrent (ALC-677). Part 107 pilots who also hold a Part 61 certificate with a current flight review can take ALC-515 instead.

The old recurrent knowledge test, UGR, was retired on April 6, 2021. You cannot take a test for recency anymore. The recency rule limits your privileges. If you let it lapse, finish the training before you act as pilot in command again.

sections.heading: Carry it, show it, keep it up to date
points: When you fly, you must have your remote pilot certificate and a photo ID in your physical possession and easy to reach. You must show them when asked by the FAA, the NTSB, TSA or any federal, state or local law enforcement officer.

The pilot in command, the owner or the person at the controls must also give the FAA, on request, any record or report that the rules require. They must allow the FAA to inspect the aircraft, the pilot and the visual observer.

If you move, you have 30 days to tell the FAA your new permanent mailing address. After 30 days you may not use the certificate's privileges until you report the change. To change your name you send the certificate and proof such as a marriage license or court order.
You can give up your certificate voluntarily. If you do, you must meet the eligibility and testing rules again to get a new one.

traps: Age: the test can be taken at 14, but the certificate needs 16. Pick the number that matches the question.
Part 107 has no medical certificate and no logbook hours. Do not choose an answer that adds either one.
Recency is not a recurrent knowledge test anymore. It is online recurrent training, or a new initial test.
24 calendar months runs to the end of the month. Do not count 730 days from the day you passed.
A failed test needs no instructor endorsement to retake. It needs only the 14-day wait and the failed test report.
A temporary certificate is real and lets you fly under Part 107 while the plastic card is in the mail.

check.q: What is the minimum age to hold a remote pilot certificate with a small UAS rating?
check.why: Section 107.61(a) sets 16 as the minimum age for the certificate. Age 14 is only the minimum to sit for the knowledge test.

check.q: A pilot passes the UAG test on September 13, 2025. By what date must the pilot finish recurrent training to keep acting as pilot in command?
check.why: The 24 months are calendar months, so the window runs to the end of the 24th month after the test, which is September 30, 2027.

check.q: A private pilot with a current flight review wants a remote pilot certificate. Which path fits?
choices: Pass the UAG test, because no other path exists.
Finish the free online Part 107 initial training, apply in IACRA and prove identity in person.
Pass a practical flight test with a designated pilot examiner.
check.why: Section 107.61(d)(2) lets a Part 61 pilot with a current flight review complete training instead of the test. Part 107 has no practical test.

check.q: A candidate fails the UAG test. What must the candidate do before retaking it?
choices: Wait 14 calendar days and show the failed test report.
Wait 30 days and finish a remedial course.

check.why: Section 107.7(a)(1) requires the certificate and identification to be in your possession and readily accessible whenever you use the certificate's privileges.

modules.title: Operating Rules: Part 107 Subpart B
modules.summary: The rules every flight must follow: who is in charge, safe condition, sight and visual observers, right of way, the four flight limits, accident reports, emergencies and waivers.
objectives: Explain the authority and duties of the remote pilot in command.
State the visual line of sight rule and the rules for visual observers.
Recall the groundspeed, altitude, visibility and cloud clearance limits.
Apply the rules on alcohol, drugs, hazardous operations, moving vehicles and hazardous material.
Decide when an accident must be reported, and what the in-flight emergency rule allows.
Name the rules that a waiver can change, and the rules that it cannot.

sections.heading: The remote pilot in command
points: A remote pilot in command, written remote PIC, must be named before or during the flight. The remote PIC is directly responsible for the operation and has the final say about it.

The remote PIC must make sure the aircraft will not be an undue hazard to people, other aircraft or property if control is lost for any reason. The remote PIC must also keep the operation within every applicable rule and must be able to direct the aircraft to stay in compliance.

Someone else may fly the controls only if that person is a certificated remote pilot, or is directly supervised by a remote PIC who can take over immediately. The remote PIC stays responsible either way.

sections.heading: Safe condition, health, alcohol and drugs
points: Before each flight the remote PIC checks the whole system to decide whether it is in a condition for safe operation. If the pilot learns or has reason to know that it is no longer safe during a flight, the flight must not continue.

The preflight actions in section 107.49 are: assess the weather, the airspace and flight restrictions, the people and property on the ground, and other ground hazards. Brief everyone who helps with the flight. Check the control links. Make sure there is enough power for the planned flight time. Make sure any attached object is secure and does not hurt controllability.
Nobody may be pilot, person at the controls, visual observer or direct participant while knowing of a physical or mental condition that would interfere with safe operation.

The pilot, the person at the controls and the visual observer must follow the alcohol and drug rules of 14 CFR 91.17 and 91.19: no flying within 8 hours of drinking alcohol, none while under the influence, none with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or more, and none while using a drug that affects your faculties.

sections.heading: Hazardous operations, moving vehicles and dangerous goods
points: You may not operate in a careless or reckless way that endangers the life or property of another. You may not let an object fall from the aircraft in a way that creates an undue hazard to people or property.

You may not operate from a moving aircraft. You may operate from a moving land or water vehicle only over a sparsely populated area, and only if the aircraft is not carrying another person's property for pay or hire.
A small unmanned aircraft may not carry hazardous material, as defined in 49 CFR 171.8.

sections.heading: Seeing the aircraft: visual line of sight and visual observers
points: With vision that is unaided except for glasses or contact lenses, the remote PIC and the person at the controls must be able to see the aircraft for the entire flight. They need to know its location, attitude, altitude and direction. They must also watch the airspace for other traffic or hazards and make sure the aircraft does not endanger anyone.
Binoculars may be used only for a moment to help awareness. First-person-view (FPV) goggles or a camera screen do not satisfy this rule.

A visual observer (VO) is optional. If you use one, the VO must be able to see the aircraft well enough to meet the rule. The remote PIC, the person at the controls and the VO must stay in effective communication at all times, and the three of them must scan for hazards and keep track of the aircraft by direct looking.
One person may not fly, or act as remote PIC or VO for, more than one unmanned aircraft at the same time.

sections.heading: Right of way and airports
points: A small unmanned aircraft must give way to all other aircraft, airborne vehicles, and launch and reentry vehicles. Giving way means you do not pass over, under or ahead of the other aircraft unless you stay well clear. You may not fly so close to another aircraft that you create a collision hazard.

You may not fly in a way that interferes with the operations and traffic patterns at an airport, heliport or seaplane base. The FAA's example: a drone hovering 200 feet above a runway can make a manned aircraft delay its takeoff or landing, and that already counts as interference even if no collision is possible.

sections.heading: The four flight limits
points: Groundspeed: no more than 87 knots, which is 100 miles per hour. Altitude: no higher than 400 feet above ground level. The exception: when you are within a 400-foot radius of a structure, you may fly up to 400 feet above that structure's highest point.

Flight visibility: at least 3 statute miles, measured from the control station. Flight visibility is the average slant distance at which you can see and identify prominent unlighted objects by day, or prominent lighted objects at night.

Distance from clouds: at least 500 feet below a cloud and at least 2,000 feet horizontally from it. Because of the 500-foot rule, a cloud layer at 600 feet above the ground leaves you only 100 feet to fly in.

sections.heading: Accident reports, inspections and in-flight emergencies
points: No later than 10 calendar days after an operation, the remote PIC must report to the FAA if the flight involved serious injury to any person, or loss of consciousness, or damage to property other than the drone. Property damage is reportable unless the repair cost, or the fair market value in a total loss, is $500 or less.
On request, you must show your certificate and identification, and let the FAA, the NTSB, law enforcement or TSA inspect the system and the people involved, as described in section 107.7.

In an in-flight emergency that needs immediate action, the remote PIC may deviate from any Part 107 rule, but only as far as needed to handle the emergency. The pilot sends a written report of the deviation only if the FAA asks for one.

sections.heading: Waivers
points: A certificate of waiver lets you depart from certain rules if you show the FAA that you can still fly safely. You follow the conditions written in the waiver. Part 107 lists which rules can be waived. Rules that are not on the list cannot be waived.

Waivable rules (section 107.205): operation from a moving vehicle or aircraft (but no waiver to carry another person's property for pay or hire), anti-collision lighting at night and twilight, visual line of sight (same limit on carrying property for pay or hire), visual observers, more than one aircraft, yielding right of way, operation over people, operation in certain airspace, the four flight limits, and operations over moving vehicles.
Rules such as the hazardous operation rule (107.23) and the alcohol and drug rule (107.27) are not on the list, so no waiver can change them.

The FAA now takes Part 107 waiver applications through the Aviation Safety Hub. Airspace authorization requests still go through FAADroneZone. Older study sources and some test items may say DroneZone for both.

numbers.value: 400 feet AGL (or 400 feet above a structure within a 400-foot radius)
3 statute miles, from the control station

numbers.item: Property damage threshold for a report
Aircraft one person may operate at once

traps: The 400-foot limit is above ground level, not mean sea level. The structure exception adds 400 feet to the structure's top, and only inside a 400-foot radius.
Visibility is measured from the control station, not from the aircraft.
The speed limit is groundspeed, not airspeed. It is 87 knots, which is about 100 miles per hour.
Seeing the drone on an FPV screen is not line of sight. Binoculars are for a moment only.
The accident report is due in 10 calendar days, and the damage threshold is $500. Injury must be serious or involve loss of consciousness.
Only a remote PIC in an emergency may break a rule, and only as much as needed. A written report is required only on request.
You do not need a visual observer by default. A VO is an option that you add.

check.q: A remote pilot inspects a 600-foot tower. Within a 400-foot radius of the tower, what is the highest the aircraft may fly without a waiver?
check.why: Inside a 400-foot radius of a structure, the limit is 400 feet above the structure's uppermost limit. 600 plus 400 is 1,000 feet AGL.

check.q: Where is the 3 statute mile minimum flight visibility measured?
check.why: Section 107.51(c) says flight visibility is observed from the location of the control station.

check.q: A remote pilot flies with FPV goggles and has no visual observer. Which statement is correct?
choices: The goggles satisfy the line of sight rule if the video is clear.
The goggles do not satisfy the rule, so the remote PIC or person at the controls must still see the aircraft directly, or a visual observer must.
The goggles satisfy the rule at night only.
check.why: Unaided vision is required. FPV devices may be used but do not meet the line of sight requirement.

check.q: A drone hits a parked car and the repair costs $1,200. Nobody is hurt. What must the remote PIC do?
choices: Report to the FAA no later than 10 calendar days after the operation.
Report to the FAA within 24 hours.
check.why: Property damage other than to the drone is reportable when repair cost or value lost is more than $500, and the report is due within 10 calendar days.

check.q: Which statement about flying from a moving land vehicle is correct?
choices: It is allowed over a sparsely populated area when the drone is not carrying another person's property for pay or hire.
It is allowed anywhere if the pilot is not the driver.
check.why: Section 107.25 allows moving land or water vehicle operations only over a sparsely populated area and only without carrying another person's property for compensation or hire. Operation from a moving aircraft is prohibited.

modules.title: Airspace, Authorizations and Flight Restrictions
modules.summary: The classes of airspace, which ones need permission, how LAANC and FAADroneZone work, special use airspace, temporary flight restrictions and NOTAMs.
objectives: Name the classes of airspace and say where each one needs ATC authorization for a drone.
Describe the shape and floor and ceiling of Class B, C and D airspace in general terms.
Tell prohibited, restricted, warning, military operations and alert areas apart, and say which ones need permission.
Explain LAANC, UAS Facility Maps, further coordination and FAADroneZone.
Find and read temporary flight restrictions and NOTAMs before a flight.

sections.heading: Controlled and uncontrolled airspace
points: Air traffic control (ATC) provides service in controlled airspace. That means Class A, B, C, D and E. Class G is uncontrolled. Class A starts at 18,000 feet MSL, far above anything a drone may reach.

The Part 107 rule is short: you need prior ATC authorization to operate in Class B, Class C or Class D airspace, or inside the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace that is designated for an airport. Everywhere else you need no airspace authorization, although every other rule still applies.
Remember the distinction: only the surface area of Class E needs authorization. The rest of Class E, and Class G, do not.

sections.heading: Class B, C, D and surface-area Class E
points: Class B surrounds the nation's busiest airports. In general it runs from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL. It is built in layers, like an upside-down wedding cake, so the floor changes as you move away from the airport.

Class C surrounds airports with an operating control tower, radar approach control and a certain level of traffic. In general it runs from the surface to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation. The usual shape is an inner circle with a 5 nautical mile radius that starts at the surface, and an outer ring out to 10 nautical miles with a floor of about 1,200 feet above the airport.

Class D surrounds airports with an operating control tower, in general from the surface up to 2,500 feet above the airport elevation. Some towers close at night. A part-time Class D area then turns into Class E surface area or into Class G, and the Chart Supplement entry for the airport says which. Check it, or let your LAANC app check it.

Surface-area Class E is controlled airspace that reaches down to the ground around an airport that has weather reporting and radio contact down to the runway but no control tower running at the time. The chart shows it with a dashed magenta line. Extensions that reach out from a surface area to hold instrument approach paths are part of the surface area, so authorization applies there too.

sections.heading: The rest of Class E and Class G
points: Class E is the controlled airspace that is not A, B, C or D. Unless the chart says otherwise, it starts 1,200 feet above the ground. Shaded edges on the chart show lower floors: a magenta edge marks a floor of 700 feet AGL, and a blue edge marks other floors where controlled airspace meets uncontrolled airspace. Over most of the country, Class E also sits above 14,500 feet MSL.

Class G is the uncontrolled airspace from the ground up to the bottom of the Class E above it. A drone pilot needs no ATC authorization in Class G. Where the Class E floor is 700 or 1,200 feet AGL, a drone that stays at or below 400 feet AGL is in Class G unless it is inside the surface area of an airport.

sections.heading: Special use airspace
points: Prohibited areas (P- numbers, for example P-40) bar all flight, for security or national welfare. Restricted areas (R- numbers) hold hazards such as artillery and guided missiles. Under section 107.45 you need permission from the using or controlling agency to enter either one.

Warning areas (W- numbers) start 3 nautical miles out from the coast, may lie over domestic or international waters, and hold activity that can hurt aircraft that are not taking part. Military operations areas (MOAs) separate military training from instrument traffic and are named, not numbered. Alert areas (A- numbers) show unusual activity, such as heavy pilot training. Controlled firing areas stop their activity when a spotter sees an aircraft near.

Part 107 does not require a drone pilot to get permission to enter a warning area, MOA or alert area. You still need to find out what is going on there and stay clear of danger. Times and altitudes for special use airspace appear in the chart margins, and in NOTAMs.

sections.heading: Other airspace and restrictions
points: Temporary flight restrictions (TFRs) protect disaster areas, large events, presidential travel and space operations. Section 107.47 makes you obey 14 CFR 91.137 through 91.145 and 99.7. Those rules cover disaster and hazard areas, Hawaii disaster areas, emergency air traffic rules, VIP movements, space flight operations, air shows and major sporting events, and special security instructions in a defense zone.

Other areas on the chart: military training routes (VR and IR routes, with speeds above 250 knots, usually below 10,000 feet MSL), national security areas, terminal radar service areas, published VFR routes, and parachute jump areas. Sports stadium TFRs can appear on the chart too.
Sectional charts do not show every restriction, so you check NOTAMs and the FAA TFR site for the day of the flight.

sections.heading: Getting authorization: UAS Facility Maps, LAANC and FAADroneZone
points: UAS Facility Maps show the highest altitudes, in a grid around each airport, where the FAA may approve Part 107 flights without more safety analysis. The maps do not authorize anything by themselves.

LAANC, the Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability, is the fast way to get authorization. You use an app from an FAA-approved UAS Service Supplier. If your request is at or below the grid altitude, you can get an approval in near real time. You can ask up to 90 days ahead. Unless the authorization says otherwise, you do not need to call the tower.

If you need to go above the grid altitude, up to 400 feet, Part 107 pilots can send a further coordination request through LAANC. An air traffic manager reviews it by hand, and requests must be sent at least 72 hours before the flight.

Airports that LAANC does not cover use FAADroneZone. Those requests are reviewed by hand at FAA service centers, and the FAA says to allow up to eight weeks. FAADroneZone requests can be for day or night.
LAANC approves airspace only. You still check NOTAMs, the weather and other restrictions yourself.

sections.heading: Flying near airports without needing authorization
points: A flight outside Class B, C, D and surface Class E does not need airspace authorization even if an airport is nearby. Section 107.43 still bans any flight that interferes with the traffic pattern or operations of any airport, heliport or seaplane base.
Stay out of traffic patterns and approach corridors. If you must fly at a small airport, keep your aircraft where a manned aircraft pilot will never have to change course to avoid it.
The FAA B4UFLY app and a current chart help you see the airspace for a site. The pilot in command must also read the Chart Supplement entry for nearby airports.

sections.heading: NOTAMs and TFR checks before every flight
points: A NOTAM, Notice to Airmen, is urgent information that is temporary or too new for a chart. Examples: air shows, parachute jumps, rocket launches, flights by important people, unlit towers, and flocks of birds (a BIRDTAM).

A TFR notice begins with the words FLIGHT RESTRICTIONS and gives the place, the time period, the area in statute miles and the altitudes. The FAA says remote pilots must check NOTAMs before each flight. The usual sources are Flight Service (1800wxbrief.com) and the FAA's TFR website, tfr.faa.gov.
Section 107.49(a) already requires you to assess the local airspace and any flight restrictions before flying, so a missed TFR is the pilot's mistake, not the app's.

numbers.value: surface to 4,000 feet above the airport; 5 nm inner ring, 10 nm outer ring from about 1,200 feet
surface to 2,500 feet above the airport

numbers.item: Class E floor, unless the chart shows another
numbers.value: 1,200 feet AGL (charted lower floors: 700 feet AGL, magenta edge)
14,500 feet MSL up to (not including) 18,000 feet MSL

traps: Only Class B, C, D and the surface area of Class E need ATC authorization. Class G and the rest of Class E do not.
A UAS Facility Map altitude is a ceiling for fast approval, not a permission. You still apply.
Special use airspace needs permission only for prohibited and restricted areas under Part 107. Do not choose that answer for MOAs.
LAANC authorizes airspace. It does not check weather, NOTAMs or TFRs for you.
A sponsor or a customer at an event does not exempt you from a TFR.
Further coordination needs the longest lead time, at least 72 hours, and is manual.

check.q: Under Part 107, in which airspace does a drone pilot need prior ATC authorization?
choices: Class B, Class C, Class D and surface-area Class E
Class G within 5 miles of an airport
check.why: Section 107.41 names Class B, C and D and the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E designated for an airport. Class G and other Class E need no authorization.

check.q: A remote pilot wants to fly at a spot where the UAS Facility Map shows 100 feet, but the job needs 300 feet. Which request fits, assuming the airport uses LAANC?
choices: A near real-time LAANC request for 300 feet
A further coordination request, sent at least 72 hours ahead
No request, because 300 feet is below 400 feet
check.why: Altitudes above the grid value, up to 400 feet, need a manually reviewed further coordination request. The FAA asks for it at least 72 hours before the flight.

check.q: Which special use airspace requires permission from the using or controlling agency under Part 107?
check.why: Section 107.45 mentions only prohibited and restricted areas. You still use caution in MOAs and alert areas.

check.q: A TFR for a sporting event covers your job site. Your company sponsors a team. May you fly?
choices: Yes, because the company is a sponsor.
Yes, if you tell everyone at the event.
No, the TFR applies to all aircraft unless you have permission such as a waiver or authorization.
check.why: Section 107.47 requires you to obey the flight restriction rules, including 91.145. A sponsor role does not change that.

check.q: Which Class C airspace statement is correct in general?
choices: It runs from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL.
It runs from the surface to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation and has an inner circle and a shelf.
check.why: The usual Class C layout is an inner circle of 5 nautical miles from the surface and an outer shelf out to 10 nautical miles, topping out at 4,000 feet above the airport.

modules.title: Reading a Sectional Chart
modules.summary: How to read altitudes, airspace lines, airports, obstacles, maximum elevation figures and coordinates on the VFR sectional chart that the test supplement uses.
objectives: Tell MSL altitudes from AGL altitudes on a chart and convert between them.
Identify Class B, C, D and E boundaries by their line style and color.
Read an airport data block and know what blue and magenta airports mean.
Read obstacle labels and the maximum elevation figure (MEF).
Find a place on the chart from latitude and longitude given in decimal degrees.

sections.heading: What a sectional chart is
points: A sectional is the standard VFR chart for pilots who fly by sight. Its scale is 1:500,000, which is large enough to read easily and wide enough to cover a good part of a state. Each chart is named after a major city in its area.
The test gives you chart pieces in a supplement book (FAA-CT-8080-2H). Each question points to a figure and an area on it, for example Figure 21, area 3. You find the area, then read the symbols.
In real life, use a current chart or an app that shows current airspace. Old charts miss new airspace, new obstacles and changed frequencies.

sections.heading: Altitudes: MSL, AGL and the missing zeros
points: Altitudes on the chart are measured above mean sea level (MSL) unless the label says AGL. Airspace labels leave off the last two zeros: a label of 40 means 4,000 feet MSL, and 12 means 1,200 feet MSL.

Class B and Class C labels are written as a fraction. The top number is the ceiling and the bottom number is the floor, both in hundreds of feet MSL. Class B figures are blue, and Class C figures are magenta. A minus sign in front of a Class D ceiling means from the surface up to but not including that altitude.
To find a height above the ground, subtract the ground elevation from the MSL altitude. Example: a Class C shelf floor of 1,200 feet MSL over ground that is 500 feet MSL is 700 feet above the ground.

sections.heading: Airspace lines you must recognize
points: Class B is a solid blue line. Class C is a solid magenta line. Class D is a dashed blue line. Class E surface area is a dashed magenta line.

Other Class E edges are shown with a soft shaded band, called a vignette. A magenta vignette means the controlled airspace floor is 700 feet above the ground. A blue vignette means a different floor where controlled airspace meets uncontrolled Class G.
Boxed notes beside an airport give the approach control frequency that arriving VFR pilots use, and notes say if the Class C or Class D area is not in effect around the clock.

Special use airspace has its own symbols: P and R areas with numbers, W for warning, A for alert, and named MOAs. Military training routes appear as thin lines. Detailed times and altitudes for special use airspace are printed at the edge of the chart.

sections.heading: Airports and their data blocks
points: Airports with a control tower and their data are printed in blue. All other airports and their data are printed in magenta. Different symbols show airports with hard-surface runways, other airports, heliports and seaplane bases.

The data block gives the airport name, the tower or common traffic advisory frequency, the field elevation in feet MSL, and the length of the longest runway in hundreds of feet. It also says if runway lights burn from dusk to dawn or if you must look up the lighting hours in the Chart Supplement.
A beacon symbol by the airport means a rotating or flashing beacon runs from dusk to dawn. Right-hand traffic pattern information is printed by the airport when a runway uses it.

The Chart Supplement, formerly called the Airport/Facility Directory, is the complete airport listing: hours, frequencies, lighting, parachute jumping and more. The chart tells you where the airport is. The Chart Supplement tells you how it works.

sections.heading: Terrain, obstacles and the maximum elevation figure
points: The chart shows terrain with contour lines, shaded relief and color tints. Basic contour lines are spaced 500 feet apart. Tight spacing means steep terrain. Color tints run from light green at low elevation to dark brown at high elevation.

Man-made obstacles that rise more than 200 feet above ground level appear as symbols, or more than 299 feet in yellow city areas. Obstacles 1,000 feet AGL or higher use a larger symbol. A number beside the symbol is the top of the obstacle in feet MSL. The height above ground is in parentheses below it. Rays around the symbol show a lit obstacle. The letters UC mean under construction.
Wind turbine blades are not lit. Their lights are on the nacelle, at the hub. Guy wires can extend outward from tall towers, so stay clear of them.

The Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF) is printed in each chart quadrant, the box between lines that fall every 30 minutes of latitude and 30 minutes of longitude. It is the highest known terrain or obstacle in that box, rounded up to the next 100 feet, with the last two digits not printed. An MEF printed as 4 over 7 means 4,700 feet MSL.

sections.heading: Finding a place with latitude and longitude
points: Latitude lines run east and west and give the distance north of the equator. Longitude lines run north and south and give the distance west of Greenwich in the United States. On a chart, north is up and longitude numbers grow as you move to the left.

Test items often give decimal degrees, such as 46.9 N and 98.6 W. Convert the decimal part to minutes by multiplying by 60: 0.9 times 60 is 54 minutes, and 0.6 times 60 is 36 minutes. So the point is 46 degrees 54 minutes north and 98 degrees 36 minutes west.

Find the latitude line, find the longitude line, and look where they cross. Then read the airspace and symbols at that spot. If the point lies inside a Class C or Class D circle or in the surface area of a Class E airport, you need ATC authorization.

sections.heading: Planning with the chart: a short routine
points: 1. Locate your site. 2. Name the airspace class that covers it, and write down the floor in feet AGL. 3. Look for airports within a few miles, towered or not. 4. Check special use airspace, military routes and TFR symbols. 5. Check the obstacles and the MEF along your route. 6. Open the NOTAMs and weather for the same time.
A phone app is a helpful second look. The chart and the Chart Supplement are what the FAA tests and what you can rely on if the app is wrong or has no signal.

numbers.value: 200 feet AGL (299 feet in yellow city tint)
30 minutes of latitude by 30 minutes of longitude
up to the next 100 feet, last two digits not printed
blue = control tower; magenta = no control tower

traps: Chart airspace numbers are hundreds of feet MSL. A label of 40 is not 40 feet and not 4,000 feet AGL.
To get AGL from MSL, subtract the elevation of the ground under the aircraft. The airport elevation is only the ground at the airport.
Class D is dashed blue and Class E surface is dashed magenta. Solid lines are B (blue) and C (magenta).
Blue airport means a control tower. Do not take blue to mean controlled airspace on its own.
The MEF is the highest feature in its box, not a safe altitude for your drone and not an AGL figure.
In the United States, longitude is west and increases to the left. Do not pick a point on the east side by mistake.

check.why: Class B is solid blue, Class C is solid magenta, Class D is dashed blue and Class E surface area is dashed magenta.

check.why: The floor is 1,200 feet MSL (the bottom number, in hundreds). Subtract the 500-foot ground elevation to get 700 feet AGL.

There is a 47-foot obstacle in the box.
check.why: The MEF is the highest feature in the quadrant, in feet MSL, rounded up to the next 100 feet, with the last two digits not printed.

check.why: Multiply the decimal part by 60. 0.9 times 60 is 54 minutes, and 0.6 times 60 is 36 minutes.

modules.title: Weather Sources and Weather Effects
modules.summary: Where to get an aviation weather briefing, how to decode METAR and TAF reports, and how density altitude, wind, stability, storms, icing and low visibility change a drone flight.
objectives: Name the free sources a remote pilot uses for weather, NOTAMs and TFRs.
Decode the parts of a METAR and a TAF.
Explain density altitude and predict how heat, altitude and humidity change performance.
Describe wind, turbulence, wind shear and microbursts, and where to expect them.
Match stable and unstable air to the weather each one brings.
Apply the visibility and cloud clearance rules to a reported ceiling.

sections.heading: Where to get weather
points: The FAA's advisory circular for Part 107 points remote pilots to three free sources. Flight Service at 1800wxbrief.com gives briefings and NOTAMs after you make a free account. The National Weather Service Aviation Weather Center at aviationweather.gov needs no account and carries METARs, TAFs and more. The FAA TFR site at tfr.faa.gov shows flight restrictions.

The telephone version of Flight Service is meant for manned aircraft pilots. Local airport weather comes from automated stations: ASOS and AWOS report wind, visibility, clouds, temperature, dew point and altimeter setting for an airport.
Your drone app's forecast is a helpful extra. It is not an aviation weather source, so check an official aviation source as well.

sections.heading: Reading a METAR
points: A METAR is the current surface weather at an airport in a standard code. It is issued on a regular schedule, and a SPECI report is issued any time conditions change quickly. Times are in Coordinated Universal Time, written with the letter Z. Zulu time is not your local time.
Example: METAR KGGG 161753Z AUTO 14021G26KT 3/4SM +TSRA BR BKN008 OVC012CB 18/17 A2970 RMK PRESFR.

Decode it in order. KGGG is the station: K plus a three-letter airport code in the 48 states. 161753Z is day 16 at 1753 UTC. AUTO means an automated source. 14021G26KT is wind from 140 degrees true at 21 knots, gusting to 26. 3/4SM is visibility three quarters of a statute mile. +TSRA BR is heavy thunderstorm with rain, and mist.

BKN008 OVC012CB is a broken layer at 800 feet and an overcast layer at 1,200 feet with cumulonimbus clouds. Cloud heights are in hundreds of feet above ground level. 18/17 is temperature 18 degrees C and dew point 17. A2970 is altimeter setting 29.70 inches of mercury. RMK PRESFR is a remark: pressure falling rapidly.

Sky cover is counted in eighths: FEW is one or two eighths, SCT is scattered (three to four), BKN is broken (five to seven), and OVC is overcast (eight, the whole sky). A ceiling is the lowest layer that is broken or overcast, or the vertical visibility into fog or haze. FEW and SCT layers are never a ceiling. Automated stations cannot detect clouds above 12,000 feet.

sections.heading: Reading a TAF and other forecasts
points: A TAF, a Terminal Aerodrome Forecast, covers the area within a 5 statute mile radius of an airport. It is valid for 24 or 30 hours and is updated four times a day, at 0000, 0600, 1200 and 1800 UTC. It uses the same codes as a METAR.

Look for FM, which marks a rapid change from a certain time. TEMPO marks a temporary change lasting less than an hour. PROB30 gives a 30 percent chance of thunderstorms or precipitation. P6SM means visibility greater than six statute miles. A TAF only shows cumulonimbus clouds in the sky group.

Convective SIGMETs warn of severe thunderstorms with surface winds above 50 knots, hail of three-quarters of an inch or more, tornadoes, and embedded or lined-up thunderstorms. A pilot report (PIREP) tells what another pilot actually saw.

sections.heading: Density altitude and performance
points: Density altitude is the altitude in the standard atmosphere that matches the actual air density. The standard atmosphere is 29.92 inches of mercury at 59 degrees F (15 degrees C) at sea level.

High density altitude means thin air and poor performance. The causes are high elevation, low pressure, high temperature and high humidity. Remember: hot, high and humid make thin air. Moist air is lighter than dry air.
Thin air means less lift and less thrust from propellers. The drone needs more power to hover, climbs slower, flies a shorter time on a charge, and may not climb at all with a heavy load.

sections.heading: Wind, turbulence and wind shear
points: Wind changes takeoff, landing and cruise. Buildings, trees, hills and cliffs break up the flow and make gusts that change quickly in speed and direction. The turbulence grows with the size of the obstacle and the strength of the wind.

On the lee side of a ridge or mountain the air follows the ground down and gets rough, and it can push an aircraft toward the ground. Valleys and canyons can have strong downdrafts. Smooth, polished-looking lenticular clouds that stand still mark mountain waves and strong turbulence.

Different ground surfaces heat the air differently. Plowed ground, rock and sand heat the air above them and make rising bumpy air. Water and trees stay cooler. That mix causes convective currents, which hurt control.

Wind shear is a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a small area. A microburst is the strongest low-level form. It is usually 1 to 2 miles across and about 1,000 feet deep, lasts 5 to 15 minutes, and can have downdrafts up to 6,000 feet per minute and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots. It starts with a headwind, then a downdraft, then a strong tailwind.

sections.heading: Stability, inversions, fronts and clouds
points: Stable air resists vertical motion. Its weather is smooth air, layered stratus clouds and fog, steady precipitation and poor visibility in haze and smoke. Unstable air lets small upward movements grow. Its weather is rough air, cumulus clouds, showers and good visibility except in blowing dust or snow.

A temperature inversion is a layer where the temperature rises with height. It is smooth and stable, and it traps haze, fog and smoke below. A low-level inversion with high humidity brings smooth air with poor visibility, fog, haze or low clouds.

The dew point is the temperature at which air is saturated. When the air temperature and dew point are close together, fog, low clouds or rain are likely. Air can reach that point by moving over a cold surface, by mixing, by cooling at night, or by being lifted.
A front is the boundary between two different air masses. Temperature, moisture and wind often change quickly across it, and storms and low-level wind shear often come with fronts.

sections.heading: Thunderstorms, icing, hail and lightning
points: A thunderstorm cell goes through three stages: cumulus (updrafts), mature (updrafts and downdrafts, precipitation begins to fall) and dissipating (downdrafts). All the hazards peak in the mature stage. Updrafts can pass 6,000 feet per minute. A cumulus cloud can build at more than 3,000 feet per minute, so do not fly in an area of rapidly growing clouds.
Thunderstorms also bring hail, lightning, tornadoes and heavy rain. A drone has no weather radar and a short range of vision. Stay away from the storm and its gust front, and land early.

Structural icing needs two things: visible moisture, such as rain or cloud droplets, and a temperature of 0 degrees C or colder where the moisture strikes the aircraft. Frost on a surface disrupts airflow and cuts lift, so remove all frost before takeoff. Dew is not a flight hazard.

sections.heading: Visibility, ceilings and the legal minimums together
points: Part 107 requires 3 statute miles of flight visibility measured at the control station. Fog, haze, rain, smoke and blowing dust can end a flight even when the METAR looks fine, because the METAR is for a station that may be miles away.

Part 107 has no minimum ceiling. It has a cloud clearance rule: stay at least 500 feet below clouds and 2,000 feet away horizontally. If the ceiling is 700 feet AGL, the highest legal altitude is 200 feet AGL. If it is 900 feet, you may fly up to the 400-foot limit.
Plan with your own limits, below the legal ones. Look at the trend in the TAF, not just the current METAR.

numbers.value: visible moisture and 0 degrees C or colder
1 to 2 miles wide, about 1,000 feet deep, 5 to 15 minutes
3/4 inch or larger hail; surface winds over 50 knots

traps: METAR times are Zulu (UTC). METAR wind is where the wind comes from, in degrees true. Heights are above ground level.
Moist air is less dense than dry air. High humidity raises density altitude and lowers performance.
High density altitude means thin air. A question can say high density altitude and ask what happens to propeller efficiency: it falls.
A ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer, not the lowest cloud. FEW and SCT are not ceilings.
Stable air is smooth but has poor visibility. Unstable air is rough but has good visibility.
A TAF covers a 5 statute mile radius around the airport, not the whole area.
Under a 700-foot ceiling, the 500-foot cloud clearance rule leaves you only 200 feet of legal altitude. The 400-foot limit does not help you there.

check.why: The first three digits are the direction the wind comes from, in degrees true. The next two digits are knots. G gives the peak gust.

check.q: Which conditions give the highest density altitude?
choices: Low elevation, low temperature, low humidity
High elevation, high temperature, high humidity
High pressure, low temperature, low humidity
check.why: High elevation, low pressure, high temperature and high humidity all thin the air and raise the density altitude.

check.why: A broken layer at 700 feet is the ceiling. You must stay 500 feet below the cloud, so 700 minus 500 gives 200 feet AGL.

check.why: Unstable air produces cumuliform clouds, showers and rough air. Smooth air with poor visibility goes with stable air.

check.q: What does a TAF describe?
choices: A forecast for the 5 statute mile radius around an airport, valid for 24 or 30 hours
The observed weather at an airport right now
A forecast for a whole state, updated once a day
check.why: A TAF is a forecast for the area within 5 statute miles of the airport. It is updated four times a day. The observation is the METAR.

modules.title: Loading and Performance
modules.summary: Weight, balance and center of gravity, load factor in turns, stability, and how to use performance data and weather to plan what the aircraft can safely do.
objectives: Explain why exceeding the maker's weight and balance limits is a safety problem.
Describe center of gravity and what changes it.
Use load factor to find how much force a turn puts on the structure, and how it raises stall speed.
Tell stability, maneuverability and controllability apart.
Use manufacturer performance data and the weather to judge what the aircraft can do.

sections.heading: Why loading matters
points: Every aircraft has weight and balance limits set by its maker or builder. Staying inside them is critical for safe flight. The maximum takeoff weight is a limit, not a promise: on a hot day, at a high elevation or with a rough launch area, the aircraft may need to carry less.

Part 107 itself limits the aircraft to less than 55 pounds, counting everything on board or attached. Section 107.49 also says that any object attached or carried must be secure and must not harm the flight characteristics or control.

Too much weight hurts nearly everything. The aircraft needs more power to lift off, climbs slower and lower, flies a shorter time and range, turns less well, and lands faster. The first sign of poor loading usually shows up at takeoff.

sections.heading: Balance and center of gravity
points: The center of gravity (CG) is the point where all the weight acts. It is not a fixed mark on the aircraft. It moves when you move or remove weight, such as a camera, a payload, a battery, or a load you drop.

The maker may give limits for where the CG must be. If the CG is outside them, the aircraft can be hard to control, even if the total weight is fine. If the CG is out of limits after loading, move or remove weight before flight.
On an airplane, lift acts at the center of pressure. Designers keep the CG forward of that point, so the aircraft tends to nose down and stays stable. A CG too far back reduces stability.

Weight can also change during a flight. The most common example on manned aircraft is burning fuel. For a drone, a released or dropped load changes both weight and balance in the middle of the flight.

sections.heading: Load factor
points: Load factor is the ratio of the lift the wing must make to the aircraft's weight. It is measured in Gs. In straight, level flight it is 1 G. In a level turn it rises with the angle of bank.

In a coordinated level turn at 60 degrees of bank, the load factor is 2 G. At 45 degrees it is about 1.4 G. At 30 degrees it is about 1.15 G. At 80 degrees it climbs to about 5.8 G. Past 45 or 50 degrees the number rises very fast. You can find it by dividing 1 by the cosine of the bank angle.

The test gives you a figure from the supplement book. You read the load factor for the bank angle and multiply it by the weight. Example: a 33-pound aircraft in a 30 degree level turn has to support about 33 times 1.15, or about 38 pounds.

sections.heading: Load factor and stall speed
points: A wing can stall at any speed if the angle of attack gets high enough. A higher load factor raises the speed at which it stalls. The stall speed grows with the square root of the load factor.

Example: an aircraft that stalls at 50 knots in straight flight stalls at 100 knots at 4 G, because the square root of 4 is 2. A bank of about 70 degrees holds 3 G, so an aircraft with a 45-knot stall speed would stall near 78 knots.
Hard turns and sudden pull-ups near the ground cause accidents because both load factor and stall speed rise at the very time you have the least room to recover.

sections.heading: Stability, maneuverability and controllability
points: Stability is the built-in tendency of the aircraft to return to its flight path after something disturbs it. It is mostly a design feature.

Maneuverability is how easily the aircraft can be maneuvered and how well it handles the stress of maneuvering. Controllability is how well it responds to the pilot's control inputs, whatever its stability. Weight, inertia, size and location of the controls, structure and power plant all affect them.
An aircraft that is very stable usually responds less quickly. Loading it heavily can reduce its response further.

sections.heading: Weather's effect on performance
points: Performance means what the aircraft can do: takeoff and landing distance, rate of climb, ceiling, payload, range, speed, maneuverability and endurance. Density altitude has a direct effect on all of them, and wind affects takeoff, landing and cruise.

Thin air from high temperature, high elevation and high humidity cuts lift and propeller thrust, so climb performance drops as density altitude rises. Adding weight on top of poor air multiplies the problem.
If the maker lists temperature or wind limits, treat them as part of the loading limits.

sections.heading: Using performance data
points: Makers publish performance data such as hover time, climb, range and endurance. The data is not standardized between makers. If your maker gives none, look for data that other users of the same model have published and treat it as a starting point.

Before a flight, match the numbers to the plan. Section 107.49 requires enough power for the whole planned flight. Anti-collision lights, a heavy payload and thin air can all cut your flight time, so plan a margin.
A good routine: weigh the loaded aircraft, check the CG, check the weather and density altitude, test hover and controls low and near you, then climb.

numbers.item: Load factor in a level turn, 60 degrees of bank
Load factor in a level turn, 45 degrees
Load factor in a level turn, 30 degrees
Load factor in a level turn, 80 degrees

numbers.value: stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor

numbers.item: Stall speed at 4 G if the 1 G stall speed is 50 knots
Standard sea level pressure for density altitude work

traps: Load factor multiplies weight. A 2 G turn doubles the force on the structure. It does not halve anything.
Stall speed does not double when load factor doubles. It rises with the square root.
Center of gravity is not a fixed point on the airframe. It moves when weight moves.
A lighter aircraft is not always safer if removing weight moves the CG out of limits.
High density altitude means low performance. A question may call it thin air, hot air or humid air.
Stable and maneuverable are different qualities. A more stable aircraft is usually less quick to respond.

modules.title: Operations Over People and at Night
modules.summary: The default ban on flying over people, the four categories that allow it, moving vehicles and open-air crowds, plus the lighting and training rules for twilight and night flights.
objectives: State the three ways a flight over a person can be legal under section 107.39.
Compare Category 1, 2, 3 and 4: weight or energy limit, paperwork, label and where each may fly.
Explain the rules for open-air assemblies and moving vehicles.
State the anti-collision light and training rules for night and civil twilight.
Apply visual line of sight, hazards and visual illusions to a night flight plan.

sections.heading: The basic rule over people
points: No one may fly a small unmanned aircraft over a human being unless one of three things is true. The person is directly participating in the operation. The person is under a covered structure or inside a stationary vehicle that gives reasonable protection from a falling aircraft. Or the operation meets one of the four categories in Subpart D.

Direct participants are the people the operation needs: the remote pilot in command, the person at the controls, visual observers and other crew. The remote PIC briefs them. Everyone else is a non-participant.

Part 107 sets no fixed stand-off distance from people. The FAA expects the remote PIC to judge it. Think about the aircraft's speed and path, what happens if it fails, the wind, and where people could walk into the area.

sections.heading: Category 1: very light aircraft
points: A Category 1 aircraft weighs 0.55 pounds (250 grams) or less on takeoff and during the whole operation, counting everything on board or attached. It must have no exposed rotating parts that could cut human skin on impact.
There is no paperwork for the maker. The remote pilot is responsible for checking the weight and the parts.

A Category 1 aircraft may not be in sustained flight over an open-air assembly of people unless the operation meets the Remote ID rules, either a standard Remote ID aircraft or a broadcast module (14 CFR 89.110 or 89.115(a)).

sections.heading: Category 2 and Category 3: tested by impact energy
points: Category 2 and 3 aircraft are heavier than Category 1 but pass a test of how hard they hit. In Category 2, the injury from an impact must be no worse than the injury from 11 foot-pounds of kinetic energy from a rigid object. In Category 3 the number is 25 foot-pounds.

Both need no exposed rotating parts that would cut skin, and no safety defects. The maker must submit a declaration of compliance (DoC) that the FAA accepts, and the aircraft must carry a permanent label that says it is eligible. The remote PIC checks that the aircraft is on an FAA-accepted DoC and has the label. The FAA keeps the list at uasdoc.faa.gov. If the label is damaged or missing, the remote PIC must relabel the aircraft before flying over people.
Category 2 may fly over people. It follows the same open-air assembly rule as Category 1: no sustained flight over an open-air assembly unless Remote ID is met.

Category 3 is more restricted. It may never fly over an open-air assembly of people. It may fly over people only in a closed or restricted-access site where everyone has been told that a drone may fly over them, or without sustained flight over any person who is not taking part, unless the person is under a covered structure or in a stationary vehicle that gives reasonable protection.
An aircraft that can change modes or configuration can qualify for more than one category only if the remote pilot cannot switch between them by accident.

sections.heading: Category 4: the aircraft has an airworthiness certificate
points: A Category 4 aircraft has an airworthiness certificate issued by the FAA under Part 21. It must be flown within the limits in its approved flight manual, and those limits must not forbid flights over people.

The owner or operator keeps the aircraft maintained to the maker's methods and keeps records of the work, the status of life-limited parts, inspections and airworthiness directives. Maintenance records must be kept for 1 year or until the work is repeated. The other records go with the aircraft when it changes owners.
Category 4 follows the same open-air assembly rule as Categories 1 and 2.

sections.heading: Open-air assemblies and moving vehicles
points: Sustained flight over an open-air assembly includes hovering over the heads of the crowd, flying back and forth over it, and circling above it. A single quick crossing that is only incidental to a point-to-point flight does not count as sustained.

For moving vehicles, a Category 1, 2 or 3 aircraft may fly over a person in a moving vehicle if the flight stays within a closed or restricted-access site and everyone in the vehicles has been told, or if the aircraft does not stay in sustained flight over the vehicles. Category 4 follows its flight manual limits.
These rules, and the open-air assembly rule, can be waived if the FAA agrees. Waivers are handled in the operating rules module.

sections.heading: Night and civil twilight rules
points: Night flight is legal without a waiver if two things are true. First, the remote PIC has completed an initial knowledge test or training, or the recurrent training, after April 6, 2021. Those versions include night operation topics. Recurrent training taken before that date does not count. Second, the aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles with a flash rate that avoids collisions.
The pilot may dim the anti-collision lights if safety calls for it, for example if the light dazzles the pilot. The lights may never be turned off.

Civil twilight needs lights too. In the continental United States civil twilight runs from 30 minutes before official sunrise to sunrise, and from official sunset to 30 minutes after sunset. The lighting rule for twilight is the same, but the training rule applies only to night. Night is the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the start of morning civil twilight. Alaska uses the Air Almanac.

sections.heading: Flying safely at night
points: Visual line of sight still applies. The aircraft's lights and the control screen cannot replace seeing the aircraft with your own eyes. At night, plan a smaller operating area so that you can keep the aircraft in sight and know its position, altitude and attitude.

Check before the flight: the anti-collision light works and the battery will last the planned time with the light on. Plan around unlit hazards on the ground such as wires, guy wires and trees. Lit towers and obstacles help, but many hazards are not lit, and wind turbine blades are not lit.
Manned aircraft show a red light on the left wing tip, a green light on the right wing tip and a white light at the tail. Seeing red and green together means the aircraft is coming toward you.

Night vision and night illusions are covered in the physiology section of the decision-making module. In short: let your eyes adapt, do not stare at one point, and keep white light away from your eyes.

modules.title: Aircraft Registration and Remote ID (14 CFR Part 89)
modules.summary: How to register and mark a Part 107 aircraft, what Remote ID is, the three ways to comply, what each one broadcasts, and what to do when the broadcast fails.
objectives: Explain which drones must be registered and how registration works for Part 107 flying.
Describe the three ways to meet the Remote ID rule.
Compare the message elements of standard Remote ID and a broadcast module.
State what the pilot must do when Remote ID stops working in flight.
Explain what ADS-B Out, FRIAs and declarations of compliance have to do with Remote ID.

sections.heading: Registering a Part 107 aircraft
points: Section 107.13 requires you to have the aircraft registration that 14 CFR 91.203(a)(2) calls for. For a small unmanned aircraft flown under Part 107, that means registering with the FAA's FAADroneZone and receiving a certificate of aircraft registration. The weight exemption for 0.55 pound drones applies only to flights that are purely recreational. A Part 107 flight needs registration at any weight.

The fee is $5 per aircraft and the registration lasts 3 years. A person must be at least 13 years old to register, and in general must be a U.S. citizen or legal permanent resident. Renew within the six months before the month it expires. A registration made under the recreational exception cannot be moved to Part 107 use, and the reverse is also true.

Keep the registration certificate, on paper or on a phone, with you when you fly. Show it to any federal, state or local law enforcement officer who asks. Update your information within 14 calendar days of a change, or when the aircraft is sold or destroyed.

sections.heading: Marking the aircraft
points: The unique identifier, normally the registration number, must be on an external surface of the aircraft, legible, and fixed so that it stays on for the whole flight. Part of the preflight check is to see that the marking is still there and readable.
If the FAA agrees, the aircraft's serial number may serve as the unique identifier.

sections.heading: What Remote ID is and who must follow it
points: Remote ID lets a drone in flight send out identification and location information that anyone nearby can receive. It helps the FAA, law enforcement and other agencies find the control station of a drone that is flying unsafely or in the wrong place.

Part 89 applies to unmanned aircraft that are registered or required to be registered, and to foreign civil drones flown in the United States. Since September 16, 2023, no one may fly such an aircraft in U.S. airspace unless the flight meets one of the compliance options.

Part 107 pilots register every device separately and each device gets its own registration number. A pilot lists the Remote ID serial number of each standard Remote ID drone or broadcast module in the registration.

sections.heading: Three ways to comply
points: 1. Standard Remote ID aircraft. The drone is built with the capability. It must broadcast from takeoff to shutdown, its serial number must be on an FAA-accepted declaration of compliance, the equipment must work and be on, and the registration must list the serial number. If the broadcast stops, the pilot must land as soon as practicable.

2. Broadcast module. A module attached to a drone that has no built-in Remote ID. The module's serial number must be on an accepted declaration of compliance and in the registration. It must broadcast directly from the aircraft. The person at the controls must be able to see the aircraft at all times, must check the module works before takeoff, and must land as soon as practicable if the broadcast stops.

3. FAA-recognized identification area (FRIA). A drone without Remote ID may fly inside a FRIA, if it and the pilot stay inside the boundary and the person at the controls can see the aircraft at all times. Only community-based organizations the FAA recognizes and educational institutions may ask for a FRIA. A FRIA lasts 48 calendar months, and a renewal request is due at least 120 days before it ends.

sections.heading: What gets broadcast
points: A standard Remote ID aircraft broadcasts: a serial number or a session ID (identity), the latitude, longitude and geometric altitude of the control station, the latitude, longitude and geometric altitude of the aircraft, the aircraft's velocity, a UTC time mark, and the emergency status of the aircraft. The control station location is the location of the person at the controls.

A broadcast module sends: the module's serial number, the aircraft's latitude, longitude, geometric altitude and velocity, the latitude, longitude and geometric altitude of the take-off location, and a UTC time mark.
The big difference: standard Remote ID reports the control station location and emergency status. A broadcast module reports the take-off location instead.

sections.heading: When the signal fails, ADS-B and Part 107
points: If a standard Remote ID aircraft or module stops broadcasting during flight, land as soon as practicable. A standard aircraft also runs a self-test before takeoff and cannot take off if its Remote ID equipment is not working.
ADS-B Out cannot be used to meet the Remote ID rule. Also, under Part 107, you may not operate with a transponder on or with ADS-B Out in transmit mode unless the FAA authorizes it.
Part 91 flights that transmit ADS-B Out under 14 CFR 91.225 are outside Part 89 subpart B.

sections.heading: Declarations of compliance, labels and foreign drones
points: The maker of a standard Remote ID aircraft or module submits a declaration of compliance to the FAA. Pilots do not submit one. A pilot checks the FAA's list of accepted declarations, at uasdoc.faa.gov, to confirm that a drone or module qualifies.
Makers must put a label on a standard Remote ID aircraft or module that says it meets Part 89. The label must be in English, legible, prominent and permanently attached.

Anyone flying a foreign-registered drone with Remote ID in the United States must first send the FAA a notice of identification. The FAA then issues a Confirmation of Identification, which is kept at the control station. This is not U.S. registration.

modules.title: Radio Communication and Airport Operations
modules.summary: Aviation radio terms and frequencies that remote pilots should understand, plus runway numbers, markings, signs, lighting, traffic patterns, security areas and wildlife at airports.
objectives: Explain why a remote pilot learns radio procedures even though Part 107 does not require radio contact.
Name the frequencies and services used at airports with and without a control tower.
Say a call sign and numbers with the phonetic alphabet and standard phraseology.
Read runway numbers, markings, signs and lights, including the airport beacon.
Describe the traffic pattern and the airport hazards that matter to a drone pilot.

sections.heading: Why a drone pilot learns aviation radio
points: A remote pilot is not required to talk to manned aircraft. You should not transmit on an active aviation frequency unless there is an emergency. But many drone flights happen near airports, and a handheld radio or scanner tuned to the airport frequency gives you traffic awareness that you cannot get any other way.
Your duty never changes: look and listen, and give way. Manned pilots at a non-towered airport are not required to make radio calls, so silence on the radio does not mean the sky is empty.

sections.heading: Frequencies and services at airports
points: A tower controls traffic at a towered airport. At an airport with no operating tower, pilots use a common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF) to announce where they are and what they plan to do. The CTAF can be a tower, Flight Service, UNICOM or MULTICOM frequency. It is printed on the chart and in the Chart Supplement.

UNICOM is an airport advisory station, often on 122.8 MHz. MULTICOM is 122.9 MHz, used at an airport that has no tower, Flight Service or UNICOM. Always confirm in the Chart Supplement or on the chart, because frequencies vary.
ATIS is a recorded broadcast of weather, active runways and notices that a busy airport updates regularly. Some airports also have automated weather, which a pilot reaches by radio.

sections.heading: How manned pilots self-announce
points: At a non-towered airport, a pilot should say the airport name, the aircraft call sign, the position and the intentions, and then repeat the airport name. A typical inbound call is made about 10 miles out, for example: Town and Country traffic, Cessna 123 Bravo Foxtrot, 10 miles south inbound for landing, Town and Country traffic.

Other calls: entering the pattern, midfield downwind, base, final, clear of the runway, and ready for departure. If you hear these calls near your site, a manned aircraft is in the pattern and your drone must give way and stay out.
Call signs for small aircraft use the make and the last letters or numbers of the registration. N123AB becomes Cessna One Two Three Alpha Bravo. Airliners use the company name and the flight number.

sections.heading: Phonetic alphabet and phraseology
points: The phonetic alphabet: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliet, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu. The digit 9 is said niner.

Altitudes are spoken in thousands and hundreds: 3,500 is three thousand five hundred. Directions are spoken as three digits in degrees: wind two seven zero at one five. Speeds are in knots. Time on the radio and in weather reports is Coordinated Universal Time, said as four digits followed by Zulu.

sections.heading: Types of airports and security areas
points: The test uses several airport types: towered airports, non-towered airports, heliports and seaplane bases. Section 107.43 applies to all of them. Do not interfere with their traffic or operations.

A Security Identification Display Area (SIDA) is a part of an airport with extra security rules, where people must display airport-issued identification. Get the airport operator's approval before you work in or near one.

sections.heading: Runway numbers, markings and signs
points: A runway number is the runway's magnetic direction in tens of degrees, rounded to the nearest whole number. Runway 27 points about 270 degrees magnetic. Letters L, C and R separate parallel runways.

Runway markings are white. Taxiway markings, hold-short markings and markings for closed or hazardous areas are yellow. A closed runway has yellow crosses at each end. A displaced threshold has white arrows leading up to a bar across the runway.

A runway holding position marking is four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed. The solid lines are on the side where aircraft must hold. Signs with a red background and white letters are mandatory instructions such as a hold-short sign. Yellow signs with black letters give directions. Black signs with yellow letters tell a pilot which taxiway they are on.

sections.heading: Airport lighting
points: The airport beacon flashes white and green for a lighted land airport, white and yellow for a lighted water airport, and green, yellow and white for a heliport. Military airports show two quick white flashes between the green. In Class B, C, D and surface Class E areas, a beacon that is on in daytime often means the visibility is less than 3 miles or the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet.

Runway edge lights are white, but on instrument runways the last 2,000 feet (or half the runway, whichever is less) are yellow. Lights at the runway ends show red toward the runway and green outward for the threshold. Taxiway edge lights are blue. Taxiway centerline lights are green.

sections.heading: Traffic patterns and wildlife
points: The standard pattern has these legs: upwind, crosswind, downwind, base and final. The usual pattern altitude is 1,000 feet above the airport for propeller aircraft and at least 1,500 feet for large and turbine aircraft. Patterns have left turns unless the chart or Chart Supplement says right traffic.

Worked example: a pilot reports midfield left downwind for runway 13. Runway 13 points about 130 degrees, toward the southeast. A left pattern lies to the left of the landing direction, which puts the aircraft northeast of the runway. On a short list of compass choices, the best fit is east.
Keep your drone out of the pattern and away from approach and departure paths, including the extended runway centerline. Manned aircraft are low and slow there.
Birds and other wildlife are a hazard for both drones and manned aircraft. Avoid flocks and nesting areas. The FAA asks that wildlife strikes be reported to its Wildlife Strike Database.
