modules.title: Emergency Procedures, Batteries and Maintenance
modules.summary: Planning for emergencies, lost links and flyaways, GPS loss, radio frequency limits, lithium battery safety, preflight inspection and maintenance of a small UAS.
objectives: Plan and brief emergency and contingency procedures before a flight.
Explain lost link, flyaway and GPS loss, and how to reduce the risk.
Name the radio bands that small UAS use and the limits of a line-of-sight link.
Handle, charge, carry and inspect lithium batteries safely.
Carry out a thorough preflight inspection and decide when an aircraft is not safe to fly.
Describe how maintenance and records work under Part 107.

sections.heading: Planning and briefing for emergencies
points: Before each flight, the remote PIC makes sure everyone who helps is told about the operating conditions, emergency procedures, contingency procedures, roles and responsibilities, and potential hazards (14 CFR 107.49(b)). The remote PIC, not an inspector or a lead observer, is the one who briefs the team.

A good plan names a place to land if things go wrong, a way for people to stay clear of the flight area, a way for the team to talk, and what each person does in each case. Contingency plans cover people or vehicles who wander into the flight area.

In an in-flight emergency the remote PIC may deviate from any Part 107 rule as far as needed to handle it, and sends a written report only if the FAA asks. An example from the FAA study guide: if a battery catches fire in flight, the pilot may climb above 400 feet AGL to reach a safe landing area.

sections.heading: Lost link and flyaways
points: A lost link, also called loss of control link, means the aircraft no longer follows commands from the controller. A flyaway is an aircraft that leaves its intended flight path and cannot be brought back. The FAA ties both to radio frequency problems, such as interference in crowded areas and obstacles that block the line-of-sight link.

Know what your aircraft does when the link is lost. Many hover, land or return to a home point. Check that the home point is right and that the return altitude clears every obstacle. Do these checks before you take off.
Before flight, check that control inputs match the aircraft's response. If controls are delayed or out of sync, the FAA says to stop flying until the control link has been inspected and tested.

sections.heading: Radio frequencies and their limits
points: Most small UAS use unlicensed radio bands: 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz (also 900 MHz in some systems). Many aircraft use 5.8 GHz for control and 2.4 GHz for video. These bands are also used by Wi-Fi, so a crowded neighborhood or office area can cause interference and trouble such as lost links or flyaways.

Both bands need a clear line of sight. Buildings, trees, hills and your own body can block the signal. Part 107 requires the remote PIC or the person at the controls to keep sight of the aircraft, which also helps keep the link line of sight.
The FCC controls radio frequencies. Unlicensed bands may be used without an FCC license. Any other band needs a license for civil users.

sections.heading: Loss of GPS
points: Many small aircraft use GPS to hold position, to return home and to respect geofences. If the signal drops, the aircraft may drift with the wind, may not hold its position, and may not be able to return home on its own.

Be ready to fly the aircraft by hand and land at once. Do not fly in places with weak GPS, such as between tall buildings or under heavy cover, unless you have practiced flying without it. Before takeoff, wait until the aircraft has acquired the number of satellites the maker requires.

sections.heading: Lithium batteries
points: Lithium batteries are highly flammable and can ignite. Fires follow a short circuit, wrong charging, extreme heat, crash damage, rough handling or a defect. A battery fire in flight can cause loss of control, so battery care is a safety matter, not just a cost matter.

Follow the maker's rules for use, charging and storage. Do not fly a battery whose case is swollen or bulging, or one that has lost much of its flight time. Both can mean the battery is about to fail, with power loss, fire or explosion.

To carry spare lithium batteries on an airline flight, the FAA says they must go in carry-on baggage only, with the terminals protected from short circuit. The usual limit is 100 watt hours per battery, and the airline may allow up to two larger ones (101 to 160 watt hours) with approval. Watt hours equal volts times amp hours. Damaged or recalled batteries must not be carried.
If a battery is hot, smoking or swelling on the ground, move it away from people and flammable items and follow the maker's guidance.

sections.heading: Preflight inspection
points: Section 107.15 requires a check of the whole system before each flight to decide if it is in a condition for safe operation. If you find a problem, fix it before flying. If you learn during flight that it is no longer safe, stop the flight.

The FAA's advisory circular lists things to look at: the airframe, propulsion, propellers, moving parts, camera and payload attachment, registration marking, control link, GPS lock, batteries for the aircraft and the controller, the display, the compass, lights if it is twilight or night, and a low-altitude test of the controls near you.

Signs the aircraft may be unsafe: cracks, delamination, leaks, strong smells of burning, soot, a changed motor sound, delayed controls, bulging batteries, shorter flight times, and loose or missing hardware.

sections.heading: Maintenance and records
points: Part 107 has no maintenance rule for most small UAS beyond the rule that the aircraft be in a condition for safe operation (section 107.15). Only Category 4 aircraft have maintenance rules (section 107.140). The FAA advises following the maker's schedule and instructions, doing unscheduled repairs when you find a problem, and not flying until the issue is fixed. If the maker requires its own technicians for a task, use them.

If a repair cannot return the aircraft or part to a safe condition, replace it. Keep records of repairs, replacements and time in service, because they help you spot patterns and show good practice. The FAA recommends them for most aircraft.

Category 4 aircraft are different. The owner must keep maintenance, life-limited part, inspection and airworthiness directive records, as covered in the over-people module. Keep software and firmware updates in your records too.

modules.summary: Risk management, the five hazardous attitudes and their antidotes, IMSAFE and PAVE, working with a crew, drugs and alcohol, stress, fatigue, dehydration, vision and night illusions.
objectives: Explain aeronautical decision-making (ADM) and the steps of risk management.
Name the five hazardous attitudes and the antidote for each.
Use the IMSAFE and PAVE checklists before a flight.
Describe crew resource management (CRM) and situational awareness for a small UAS crew.

sections.heading: Aeronautical decision-making and risk management
points: Aeronautical decision-making (ADM) is a step-by-step way to decide the best action in a given situation, using the latest information. The FAA teaches that good judgment can be learned. It does not simply grow with experience.

The steps are: identify attitudes that are hazardous to safe flight, learn how to change behavior, recognize and cope with stress, build risk assessment skills, use all resources, and judge how well your own ADM is working.

A hazard is a real or perceived condition that a pilot meets. Risk is the pilot's assessment of that hazard. Four risk management principles: accept no unnecessary risk; make risk decisions at the right level; accept risk when the benefits outweigh the costs; and build risk management into planning at all levels.

A safety culture grows when a team recognizes hazardous attitudes and writes standard operating procedures that stress safety. Risk management is the method for breaking the chain of events before an accident happens.

sections.heading: The five hazardous attitudes
points: Anti-authority: 'Don't tell me.' Antidote: Follow the rules. They are usually right.
Impulsivity: 'Do something quickly.' Antidote: Not so fast. Think first. An order such as fly first, ask questions later is an impulsive attitude.
Invulnerability: 'It won't happen to me.' Antidote: It could happen to me.
Macho: 'I can do it.' Antidote: Taking chances is foolish. This is the attitude of taking risks to impress others.
Resignation: 'What's the use?' Antidote: I am not helpless. I can make a difference.
To fight a hazardous attitude, first notice it, label it as hazardous, and then say the antidote.

sections.heading: Checklists: IMSAFE and PAVE
points: IMSAFE checks the pilot: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion. Stress is not on the list of medical conditions that ground a pilot, but it can still ruin your judgment.
PAVE sorts the risks of a flight into four groups: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment and External pressures. Weather, terrain and airspace go under environment.

External pressure is the single biggest key to risk management because it can make a pilot ignore every other risk. Examples: the wish to impress someone, the client waiting, and the goal of finishing the job. Set personal minimums and standard operating procedures before the pressure arrives. Probably the two most dangerous words in aviation are 'Watch this!'

sections.heading: Crew resource management and situational awareness
points: Crew resource management (CRM) is the effective use of all resources: people, equipment and information. For a UAS crew, the people are the remote PIC, the person at the controls, the visual observers and anyone else on the team.
CRM must be built into every phase of the operation, not just the flight itself. The parts are effective team communication, task management and situational awareness.

Brief the crew before the flight. Agree on roles, on how people will talk, and on what each person does if something goes wrong. Speak up when you see a hazard. Watch for task overload and tunnel vision on the screen while the airspace goes unscanned.

Situational awareness means knowing what is happening around you now and what is likely to happen next. Single-pilot resource management uses the same ideas for a person working alone: task management, automation management and good decisions.

sections.heading: Alcohol, drugs and medication
points: You may not fly within 8 hours after drinking alcohol, while under the influence, or with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or more. Eight hours is the minimum. A hangover means you are still impaired, and a lot of alcohol can stay in the body more than 16 hours.

You may not fly while using a drug that affects your faculties in a way contrary to safety. Cold and allergy medicines, especially antihistamines and decongestants, can cause drowsiness. The FAA study guide advises waiting at least 48 hours after the first dose of a new medicine, to see whether it has side effects, before flying.
The remote PIC is also responsible for the visual observers and others on the crew. Nobody on the crew may be impaired.

sections.heading: Stress, fatigue, dehydration, heat and hyperventilation
points: Fatigue is a frequent cause of pilot error. It cuts attention, coordination and decision-making. Acute fatigue is cured by rest, but chronic fatigue is not. Fatigue leaves you in an impaired state, and even an experienced pilot may not notice it. If you are tired, do not fly.

Stress releases hormones, raises heart rate and breathing, and narrows your attention. Acute stress comes from an immediate threat. Chronic stress builds from long-term pressure and makes performance fall sharply.

Hyperventilation is breathing too fast and deep, which blows off too much carbon dioxide. Symptoms include dizziness, tingling, muscle spasms and blurred vision. The cure is to slow your breathing, by breathing normally, talking aloud or breathing into a paper bag.

Dehydration lowers performance. Signs are headache, fatigue, cramps, sleepiness and dizziness. Drink two to four quarts of water a day, and do not wait until you feel thirsty. Heatstroke is the body's loss of temperature control. In hot work, drink about a pint an hour in moderate heat and a quart an hour in severe heat, and take shade breaks.

sections.heading: Vision, scanning and night illusions
points: Scan the sky in steps: look in blocks about 30 degrees wide, stop for no more than 2 to 3 seconds at each block, and overlap each new block by about 10 degrees. Start at the greatest distance and work in toward the aircraft's position.

Cones in the center of your eye see color and detail but work poorly in dim light. Rods work in the dark and handle your side vision. At night, the center of the field has a blind spot. Look about 5 to 10 degrees off to the side of an object to see it. If you stare at the object more than 2 to 3 seconds it fades, so keep your eyes moving.

Rods need about 30 minutes to adapt fully to the dark. A bright light can destroy that adaptation in a moment. Keep lights low when you prepare the aircraft, and keep bright lights off the flight line. Wearing sunglasses in bright sun beforehand also helps.

At night you also lose some sharpness, color and depth perception, and your judgment of size can drift. Lack of oxygen reduces night vision measurably above about 4,000 feet pressure altitude, so a high site makes it worse.

Two night illusions to know: autokinesis, where a steady light stared at in the dark seems to move, and false horizon, where a dark scene with scattered lights, an obscured horizon or sloping clouds fools you about the true horizon. Use reliable, fixed points on the ground as references, and keep your eyes moving.

traps: Fly first, ask questions later is impulsivity. Taking risks to impress others is macho. It won't happen to me is invulnerability.
IMSAFE is for the pilot. PAVE is for the whole flight. Do not mix them up.
The single biggest key to risk management in PAVE is external pressure.
Eight hours is a minimum. It is not a promise that you are fine.
Staring at a night object makes it disappear. Look to the side and keep moving.
A bright flashlight ruins dark adaptation. Rods need about 30 minutes to recover.
Thirst is a late sign of dehydration. Drink before you feel it.

choices: Slow the breathing rate, for example by breathing normally or talking aloud.

test_day: Bring a government-issued photo ID. It must show your photo, signature, date of birth and permanent mailing address.
Have your FAA Tracking Number (FTN) from IACRA ready before you arrive. Arrive early.
Leave notes and books at home. The testing center gives you the supplement book with the figures.
A simple calculator is allowed. Written or electronic notes are not.
You have 2 hours for 60 questions, which is about 2 minutes per question. Answer every question, mark the hard ones, and come back if you have time.
For chart questions, find the figure and area the question names, then read the symbol, the line style and the numbers before you look at the choices.
Keep your test report. You need the 17-digit exam ID to finish your application in IACRA.
after: Finish Form 8710-13 in IACRA with your exam ID. Watch for the TSA email that lets you print a temporary certificate. A temporary certificate is good for up to 120 calendar days.
Carry your remote pilot certificate and a photo ID every time you fly.
Register each drone you fly under Part 107 in FAADroneZone, put the registration number on the outside of the aircraft, and list each Remote ID serial number.
Set a reminder for your recurrent training. It is free on FAASafety.gov and due within 24 calendar months of your last test or training.
Install a LAANC app from an FAA-approved UAS Service Supplier before you need it.
Report a new address to the FAA within 30 days.
Apply for a waiver if your work needs something Part 107 does not allow. Check state and local laws too, because they can apply as well.
